summary:
A merge-sort count where the counting rule (`a > 2b`) differs from the merge rule (`a <= b`), so count in a
separate pass before each merge: with both halves sorted, a pointer into the right half only moves forward as
the left values grow. O(n log n), with 64-bit arithmetic for `2 · price`.

question.md:
Count pairs of days `i < j` with `prices[i] > 2 · prices[j]`.

- **Prices span the whole 32-bit range**, negatives included, so `2 · price` overflows 32-bit integers.
- **Up to 5 × 10⁴ prices.**

think.md:
Prices `[7, 3, 10, 2, 1, 6]`: the big drops are (7, 3), (7, 2), (7, 1), (3, 1), (10, 2), (10, 1), so **6**.

Like counting inversions, split the list: pairs inside each half are counted recursively; pairs across the halves
are easy when both halves are sorted. For a left value `x`, the right values that qualify are those below
`x / 2`: a prefix of the sorted right half. And as `x` grows, that prefix only grows, so one pointer sweeps the
right half once per merge.

The twist compared with inversions: the merge itself uses `<=`, a different test, so do the counting sweep
first, then merge.

idea.md: Double loop over `i < j`, counting `prices[i] > 2 · prices[j]` in 64-bit.

lines.text: Every pair; `2 · prices[j]` is computed in 64 bits so it can't overflow.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²):** about 1.25 × 10⁹ pairs for 5 × 10⁴ prices. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: 2 is more than double nothing later.
1 is more than double nothing later.
6 is more than double nothing later.

walk.title: Check every pair i < j for prices[i] > 2 · prices[j].

limits.md: Too many pairs. As with inversions, sorted halves let one forward-moving pointer count all cross pairs in linear time.

approaches.title: Merge sort with a counting sweep

idea.md: Merge sort a copy. Before each merge of sorted `[lo, mid)` and `[mid, hi)`: keep `j` at `mid`; for each `i` in the left half (increasing), advance `j` while `a[i] > 2 · a[j]`, and add `j − mid`. Then merge as usual.

build: Recursive merge sort with a buffer.
Counting sweep with a forward pointer.

lines.text: A copy to sort and a buffer.
Pairs within each half, counted recursively.
Both halves are sorted. For bigger left values, more right values qualify, so `j` only moves forward: O(length) for the whole sweep. `2 · a[j]` in 64 bits.
Then an ordinary merge, so the parent call gets a sorted range.

steps.text: Halves [3] and [10]: the pointer only moves forward, as left values grow. +0. Then merge.
Halves [7] and [3, 10]: the pointer only moves forward, as left values grow. +1. Then merge.
Halves [1] and [6]: the pointer only moves forward, as left values grow. +0. Then merge.
Halves [2] and [1, 6]: the pointer only moves forward, as left values grow. +0. Then merge.
Halves [3, 7, 10] and [1, 2, 6]: the pointer only moves forward, as left values grow. +5. Then merge.

walk.title: Merge sort. Before merging two sorted halves, count cross pairs with two pointers: for each left value, how many right values are less than half of it.

takeaways.md:
- When the **counting condition differs from the sort order**, count in a separate two-pointer sweep before
  merging.
- Sorted halves make "how many on the right satisfy this" a monotone pointer.
- Watch overflow: doubling a 32-bit value needs 64 bits.
